[Howard Schultz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Schultz "Howard Schultz") was chief executive from 1986 to 2000, and again from 2008 to 2017.

**Starbucks Corporation** is an American multinational [chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coffeehouse_chains "List of coffeehouse chains") of [coffeehouses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffeehouse "Coffeehouse") and [roastery reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starbucks_Reserve "Starbucks Reserve") headquartered in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"), Washington. It was founded in 1971 by [Jerry Baldwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Baldwin "Jerry Baldwin"), [Zev Siegl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zev_Siegl "Zev Siegl"), and [Gordon Bowker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Bowker "Gordon Bowker") at Seattle's [Pike Place Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pike_Place_Market "Pike Place Market") initially as a [coffee bean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee_bean "Coffee bean") wholesaler. Starbucks was converted into a coffee shop serving [espresso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espresso "Espresso")-based drinks under the ownership of [Howard Schultz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Schultz "Howard Schultz"), who was chief executive officer from 1986 to 2000 and led the aggressive expansion of the franchise across the [West Coast of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_of_the_United_States "West Coast of the United States").

As of November 2022,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Starbucks&action=edit) the company had 35,711 stores in 80 countries, 15,873 of which were located in the United States. Of Starbucks' U.S.-based stores, over 8,900 are company-operated, while the remainder are licensed.[[4]](#cite_note-:3-4) It is the [world's largest coffeehouse chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coffeehouse_chains "List of coffeehouse chains"). The company is ranked 120th on the [*Fortune* 500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_500 "Fortune 500")[[5]](#cite_note-5) and 303rd on the [*Forbes* Global 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes_Global_2000 "Forbes Global 2000"),[[6]](#cite_note-6) as of 2022.

The rise of the [second wave of coffee culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_wave_of_coffee#History "Third wave of coffee") is generally attributed to Starbucks, which introduced a wider variety of coffee experiences. Starbucks serves hot and cold drinks, whole-bean coffee, micro-ground [instant coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instant_coffee "Instant coffee"), [espresso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espresso "Espresso"), [caffe latte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caffe_latte "Caffe latte"), full and loose-leaf [teas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea "Tea"), juices, [Frappuccino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frappuccino "Frappuccino") beverages, [pastries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastries "Pastries"), and snacks. Some offerings are seasonal or specific to the locality of the store. Depending on the country, most locations provide free [Wi-Fi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi-Fi "Wi-Fi") Internet access. The company has been subject to [multiple controversies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criticism_of_Starbucks "Criticism of Starbucks") related to its business practices. Conversely, its franchise has commanded substantial [brand loyalty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brand_loyalty "Brand loyalty"), market share, and [company value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valuation_(finance) "Valuation (finance)").

## History

### 20th century

#### 1970s

Starbucks originally opened in Seattle, Washington, on March 30, 1971.[[7]](#cite_note-7) By selling [coffee beans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee_bean "Coffee bean") and related equipment, Starbucks became a local coffee bean retailer for the first ten years in Seattle.[[8]](#cite_note-8) It was founded by business partners [Jerry Baldwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Baldwin "Jerry Baldwin"), [Zev Siegl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zev_Siegl "Zev Siegl") and [Gordon Bowker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Bowker "Gordon Bowker") who first met as students at the [University of San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_San_Francisco "University of San Francisco").[[9]](#cite_note-9) The trio were inspired to sell high-quality coffee beans and equipment by coffee roasting entrepreneur [Alfred Peet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Peet "Alfred Peet").[[10]](#cite_note-Pren2523-10) Bowker recalls that a business partner of his, Terry Heckler, thought words beginning with the letters "st" were powerful, leading the founders to create a list of words beginning with "st", hoping to find a brand name. They chose "Starbo", a misreading of the mining town Storbo in the [Cascade Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cascade_Range "Cascade Range") named after Peter Storbo, founder and president of the Mount Rainier Mining Company.[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12) From there, the group remembered "Starbuck", the name of the [chief mate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_mate "Chief mate") in the book *[Moby-Dick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moby-Dick "Moby-Dick").*[[13]](#cite_note-gotitsname-13) Bowker said, "*Moby-Dick* didn't have anything to do with Starbucks directly; it was only coincidental that the sound seemed to make sense*.*"[[13]](#cite_note-gotitsname-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14)

The first Starbucks store was located in Seattle, at 2000 Western Avenue, from 1971 to 1976. The café was later moved to 1912 Pike Place.[[15]](#cite_note-15) During this time, Starbucks stores sold just coffee beans and not drinks.[[16]](#cite_note-16) In its first two years of operation, Starbucks purchased green coffee beans from [Peet's Coffee & Tea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peet's_Coffee_&_Tea "Peet's Coffee & Tea"). In 1973, Alfred Peet stopped supplying Starbucks and helped train their new Roastmaster, Jim Reynolds.[[17]](#cite_note-peets.com-17)

#### 1980s

The first Starbucks to sell brewed coffee opened in 1982. Later that year, the company hired [Howard Schultz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Schultz "Howard Schultz"), who was behind the push to begin selling brewed coffee. The company opened its first espresso bar in 1984.[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-StarbucksIlGIornale-19)

That year, the original owners of Starbucks, led by [Jerry Baldwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Baldwin "Jerry Baldwin"), purchased [Peet's Coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peet's_Coffee "Peet's Coffee").[[20]](#cite_note-20) By 1986, the company was operating six stores in Seattle and had begun to sell [espresso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espresso "Espresso") coffee.[[21]](#cite_note-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22)

Since the founders did not wish to expand too far from their original goal of that centered upon selling arabica coffee beans, Schultz left the company in 1985 to found Il Giornale, a cafe inspired by the coffee bars he observed in [Milan, Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan,_Italy "Milan, Italy"). Starbucks was the first investor in this venture, which used its beans in its beverages.[[19]](#cite_note-StarbucksIlGIornale-19) In 1987, the original owners sold the Starbucks chain to Schultz, their former director of marketing, who rebranded his Il Giornale coffee outlets as Starbucks and began to expand the company.[[23]](#cite_note-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24) Also in 1987, Starbucks opened its first locations outside of Seattle, in [Waterfront Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterfront_Station_(Vancouver) "Waterfront Station (Vancouver)") in [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver"), British Columbia, and in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), Illinois.[[25]](#cite_note-tele40-25)

By 1989, there were 46 Starbucks stores located across the [Pacific Northwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Northwest "Pacific Northwest") and [Midwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwest "Midwest"), and the company was roasting more than 2,000,000 pounds (907,185 kg) of coffee annually.

#### 1990s

In June 1992, at the time of its [initial public offering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering"), Starbucks (ticker symbol: SBUX) had 140 outlets, with revenue of US$73.5 million, up from US$1.3 million in 1987. The company's market value was US$271 million by this time.[[26]](#cite_note-26) The 12% portion of the company that was sold raised around US$25 million for the company, which enabled it to double its number of stores over the next two years.[[27]](#cite_note-27) In 1994, Starbucks acquired [The Coffee Connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Coffee_Connection "The Coffee Connection"), gaining the rights to use, make, market, and sell the "[Frappuccino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frappuccino "Frappuccino")" beverage.[[28]](#cite_note-chilly-28) The beverage was introduced under the Starbucks name in 1995.

In 1999, Starbucks experimented by opening eateries in the [San Francisco Bay Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay_Area "San Francisco Bay Area"), under the Circadia restaurant brand.[[29]](#cite_note-circadia-29) At the same time, Starbucks converted its Seattle Circadia restaurant into a Café Starbucks.[[29]](#cite_note-circadia-29) The same year, Starbucks acquired Pasqua Coffee—a [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco")-based retail coffee chain that had almost 60 locations in San Francisco, Los Angeles, and New York City.[[30]](#cite_note-Clark-30)

### 21st century

#### 2000s

In April 2003, Starbucks acquired [Seattle's Best Coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle's_Best_Coffee "Seattle's Best Coffee") and [Torrefazione Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torrefazione_Italia "Torrefazione Italia") from [AFC Enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFC_Enterprises "AFC Enterprises") for US$72 million. The deal only gained 150 stores for Starbucks, but according to the *[Seattle Post-Intelligencer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Post-Intelligencer "Seattle Post-Intelligencer"),* the wholesale business was more significant.[[31]](#cite_note-31) By June 2003, Starbucks Japan had 466 stores and would add another 70 to 75 in the 2003 financial year. Its president, Yuji Tsunoda said it would install ovens in all stores to improve its food offerings.[[32]](#cite_note-auto-32)

From 2005 to 2007, [Howard Behar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Behar "Howard Behar") served as the president of Starbucks North America.[[33]](#cite_note-33) In September 2006, rival [Diedrich Coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diedrich_Coffee "Diedrich Coffee") announced that it would sell most of its company-owned retail stores to Starbucks, including most locations of Oregon-based Coffee People, escalating regional [coffee wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee_wars "Coffee wars"). Starbucks converted the Diedrich Coffee and Coffee People locations to Starbucks. The Coffee People locations at [Portland International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_International_Airport "Portland International Airport") were excluded from the sale.[[34]](#cite_note-34)

In early 2008, Starbucks started a community website, My Starbucks Idea, designed to collect suggestions and feedback from customers. Other users could comment and vote on suggestions. Journalist Jack Schofield noted that "My Starbucks seems to be all sweetness and light at the moment, which I don't think is possible without quite a lot of censorship."[[35]](#cite_note-35) In March 2008, Starbucks acquired [Coffee Equipment Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee_Equipment_Company "Coffee Equipment Company"), which was the manufacturer of the Clover Brewing System. It began testing the "fresh-pressed" coffee system at several Starbucks locations in Seattle, California, New York, and Boston.[[36]](#cite_note-Tasting-36)

In July 2008, during the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession"), Starbucks announced it was closing 600 underperforming company-owned stores and cutting U.S. expansion plans amid growing economic uncertainty.[[37]](#cite_note-37)[[38]](#cite_note-38) On July 29, 2008, Starbucks also cut almost 1,000 non-retail jobs as part of its bid to re-energize the brand and boost its profit. Of the new cuts, 550 of the positions were layoffs and the rest were unfilled jobs.[[39]](#cite_note-39) Additionally in July 2008, Starbucks announced that it would close 61 of its 84 stores in Australia in the following month.[[40]](#cite_note-40) Nick Wailes, an expert in strategic management of the [University of Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sydney "University of Sydney"), said that "Starbucks failed to truly understand Australia's café culture."[[41]](#cite_note-41)

In January 2009, Starbucks announced the closure of an additional 300 underperforming stores and the elimination of 7,000 positions. CEO Howard Schultz also announced that he had received board approval to reduce his salary.[[42]](#cite_note-42) Altogether, from February 2008 to January 2009, Starbucks terminated an estimated 18,400 U.S. jobs and began closing 977 stores worldwide.[[43]](#cite_note-43) In August 2009, [Ahold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahold "Ahold") announced closures and rebranding for 43 of its licensed store Starbucks kiosks for their US-based [Stop & Shop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stop_&_Shop "Stop & Shop") and [Giant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant-Landover "Giant-Landover") supermarkets.[[44]](#cite_note-44)[[45]](#cite_note-45)

#### 2010s

In 2012, Starbucks had annual Frappuccino sales of over US$2 billion.[[28]](#cite_note-chilly-28) In August 2012, the largest Starbucks in the US opened at the University of Alabama's Ferguson Centre.[[46]](#cite_note-46) On June 25, 2013, Starbucks began to post [calorie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calorie "Calorie") counts on menus for drinks and pastries in all of its U.S. stores.[[47]](#cite_note-47) In July 2013, more than 10% of in-store purchases were made on customers' mobile devices via the Starbucks app.[[48]](#cite_note-48)

The company once again utilized the mobile platform when it launched the "Tweet-a-Coffee" promotion in October 2013. On this occasion, the promotion also involved [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") and customers were able to purchase a US$5 gift card for a friend by entering both "@tweetacoffee" and the friend's handle in a [tweet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tweet_(social_media)#Tweets "Tweet (social media)"). Research firm Keyhole monitored the progress of the campaign; a December 2013 media article reported that 27,000 people had participated and US$180,000 of purchases had been made to date.[[49]](#cite_note-49)[[50]](#cite_note-50)

In January 2014, as part of a change in compact direction, Starbucks management transitioned from a singular brand worldwide to focusing on locally relevant design for each store.[[51]](#cite_note-51) In May 2014, Starbucks announced ongoing losses in the Australian market, which resulted in all remaining stores being sold to the Withers Group.[[52]](#cite_note-52) In July 2017, Starbucks acquired the remaining 50% stake in its Chinese venture from long-term joint venture partners Uni-President Enterprises Corporation (UPEC) and President Chain Store Corporation (PCSC) for US$1.3 billion.[[53]](#cite_note-53)[[54]](#cite_note-54)

On March 21, 2018, Starbucks announced that it was considering the use of [blockchain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockchain "Blockchain") technology to connect coffee drinkers with coffee farmers who could eventually be able to take advantage of new financial opportunities. The [pilot program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot_program "Pilot program") was planned to start with farmers in [Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica "Costa Rica"), Colombia, and Rwanda in order to develop a new way to track the bean-to-cup journey.[[55]](#cite_note-55) In 2019, at the [Microsoft Build conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Build_(developer_conference) "Build (developer conference)"), the coffee company formally announced its "bean to cup" program using the [Microsoft's Azure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Azure "Microsoft Azure")-based blockchain service.[[56]](#cite_note-56)

Two men were arrested in a Philadelphia Starbucks location after a manager claimed the two were trespassing on April 12, 2018.[[57]](#cite_note-57) The arrests led to protests due to their apparently racially motivated nature. CEO [Kevin Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Johnson_(executive) "Kevin Johnson (executive)") later apologized for the incident, and the company declined to press charges.[[58]](#cite_note-58) During the company's second quarter earnings call on April 26, Johnson indicated that the company had not seen a drop in sales as a result of the event and subsequent coverage.[[59]](#cite_note-59) The company reiterated its guidance for full year earnings,[[60]](#cite_note-60) and beat consensus expectations of 1.8 percent same-store sales growth, with 2 percent growth.

Johnson announced that the company would close some 8000 locations on May 29 for a seminar about racial bias in order to prevent future events similar to those that occurred in Philadelphia.[[61]](#cite_note-61) On June 19, 2018, Starbucks announced the closing of 150 locations in 2019, three times the number the corporation typically closes in a single year. The closings were to happen in [urban areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas "Urban areas") that already have dense clusters of stores.[[62]](#cite_note-62)

In July 2019, Starbucks announced that it would no longer be selling newspapers in its cafés. It was also announced that kiosks for grab-and-go snacks and bags of whole-bean coffee would be removed from stores beginning in September 2019.[[63]](#cite_note-63) In November 2019, Starbucks opened its largest store ever on [Michigan Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Avenue_(Chicago) "Michigan Avenue (Chicago)"), Chicago, with 200 employees.[[64]](#cite_note-64)

#### 2020s

On March 20, 2020, due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), Starbucks closed all the café-only stores in the United States for two weeks. During that time, only drive-thru and delivery-only services were to function. According to the company representatives, all workers were to be paid for the next 30 days whether they went to work or stayed home.[[65]](#cite_note-65) COVID-19 lockdowns caused Starbucks to suffer a general 10% sales decrease, and a 50% decrease in China where quarantine measures were especially strict.[[66]](#cite_note-66) In May 2020, the company asked for reduced rent from landlords due to the decrease in sales.[[67]](#cite_note-67)[[68]](#cite_note-68)[[69]](#cite_note-69)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Starbucks_Pick_Up_NYC.jpg/250px-Starbucks_Pick_Up_NYC.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Starbucks_Pick_Up_NYC.jpg)

A Starbucks Pick Up location in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City")

In June 2020, during the [COVID-19 pandemic in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), the company announced that it would close 400 of its locations in the US/Canada region over the subsequent 18 months as it moves from the coffee house concept to "convenience-led" formats with [drive-through](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drive-through "Drive-through") and [curbside pickup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curbside_pickup "Curbside pickup"). Starbucks announced that it planned to open 300 stores that would primarily focus on carryout and pickup orders.[[70]](#cite_note-70)[[71]](#cite_note-71) The new stores would work with the Starbucks [mobile app](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_app "Mobile app") for prepayment by the customer before arrival to pick up the order. The layout of some stores would also be modified with a separate counter for picking up mobile orders. In December 2020, Starbucks announced that it is planning to increase its store count to about 55,000 by 2030, up from roughly 33,000.[[72]](#cite_note-72)

Bloomberg reported in July 2022 that the company was, through investment bank [Houlihan Lokey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houlihan_Lokey "Houlihan Lokey"), exploring selling its stores in the United Kingdom.[[73]](#cite_note-73) In August 2022, after months of suspension due to the [Russian invasion of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine") and the [Russo-Ukrainian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Ukrainian_war_(2022–present) "Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present)"), Starbucks sold all its stores in Russia to the Russian rapper [Timati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timati "Timati"). The stores were rebranded as "Stars Coffee", and are very similar to the former stores. Starbucks said it had no comment on the new owner.[[74]](#cite_note-74)[[75]](#cite_note-75) On October 1, 2022, [Howard Schultz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Schultz "Howard Schultz") stepped down as CEO, with [Laxman Narasimhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laxman_Narasimhan "Laxman Narasimhan") becoming Starbucks's next CEO.[[76]](#cite_note-76)

On March 23, 2023, Narasimhan told employees that he would work a half-day behind a store counter each month, and he trained as a barista to immerse himself in the brand and stay close to customers.[[77]](#cite_note-77) In June 2023, Starbucks was ordered to pay $25 million in punitive damages and $600,000 compensatory damages to a former regional manager. The court found that Starbucks fired her in 2018 because she was white.[[78]](#cite_note-78) In December 2023, the operator of all of the Starbucks locations in Brazil, SouthRock Capital, declared itself bankrupt. SouthRock would continue to operate Starbucks locations normally while closing a few underperforming ones and would restructure through the bankruptcy procedure.[[79]](#cite_note-79) SouthRock Capital later declared [Chapter 15 bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_15_bankruptcy "Chapter 15 bankruptcy") in June 2024.[[80]](#cite_note-80)

On August 13, 2024, Starbucks announced it was replacing then CEO Laxman Narasimhan with [Brian Niccol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Niccol "Brian Niccol"). Niccol had served as the CEO of [Chipotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chipotle_Mexican_Grill "Chipotle Mexican Grill") since 2018. In January 2025, Starbucks ended its 'open-door policy', and requires customers to make a purchase in order to use restrooms and the seating area.[[81]](#cite_note-81)[[82]](#cite_note-82) In February 2025, Starbucks cut 30% of its menu in an effort to simplify its processes and reduce costs. The discontinued offerings were primarily less popular or more complex items, including some Frappuccino blended drinks, Royal English Breakfast Latte, and White Hot Chocolate.[[83]](#cite_note-83) In July 2025, Starbucks announced corporate office employees would have to return to working physically in the office four days per week, starting in October. For workers who would prefer to instead leave the company, Starbucks would offer a one-time voluntary exit program which would include a cash payment.[[84]](#cite_note-84)

In January 2026, Starbucks announced their turnaround strategy which involved forming a joint venture with [Boyu Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyu_Capital "Boyu Capital") to run its business in China, the company’s second-largest market. After the deal closes in the second quarter of fiscal 2026, pending regulatory approval, Boyu will hold up to a 60% interest in the joint venture.[[85]](#cite_note-85)

In March 2026, Starbucks announced plans for new regional corporate offices, making a massive expansion by establishing a major corporate hub in Nashville, Tennessee. The company is investing $100 million into this new regional headquarters, which will house up to 2,000 employees over the next five years.[[86]](#cite_note-86)

##### American unionization efforts

Main article: [Starbucks unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starbucks_unions "Starbucks unions")

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Starbucks_Workers_Rally_and_March_01.jpg/250px-Starbucks_Workers_Rally_and_March_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Starbucks_Workers_Rally_and_March_01.jpg)

Starbucks workers protesting in Seattle

Three of the company's stores in [Buffalo, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo,_New_York "Buffalo, New York") began an attempt to unionize in August 2021.[[87]](#cite_note-wsj_0921-87) Using [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter"), the workers announced they had formed an organizing committee, Starbucks Workers United, to form a union affiliated with [Workers United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workers_United "Workers United").[[88]](#cite_note-88) Two more stores joined the effort in September, however these petitions were later withdrawn to ensure a speedy process for the original three locations.[[89]](#cite_note-89)[[90]](#cite_note-90)[[91]](#cite_note-91) During the union drive, the company sent other managers and executives, including its North America retail president, to Buffalo to engage with employees about operational issues and participate in their work. Employees were forced to attend [captive audience meetings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captive_audience_meeting "Captive audience meeting") that contained anti-union messages.[[92]](#cite_note-92) Starbucks temporarily closed some area stores for remodeling and added excessive staff to one of the stores preparing to vote. Workers said this reduced union support there, while Starbucks said the support was meant to compensate for increased sick leave during the pandemic as it had done elsewhere in the country.[[93]](#cite_note-symbolic-93) On November 9 Workers United filed three more petitions for elections to represent workers at additional Buffalo area stores.[[94]](#cite_note-94) On November 10 the [National Labor Relations Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Labor_Relations_Board "National Labor Relations Board") mailed out votes for the elections at the original three locations.[[95]](#cite_note-:0-95) Votes for the original three stores were counted on December 9.[[96]](#cite_note-96) Days before the vote count, the NLRB rejected arguments by Starbucks to halt the election.

Inspired by their colleagues in Buffalo, workers at a Starbucks store in Mesa, Arizona, petitioned the NLRB for a union election on November 18, 2021, to be represented by Workers United. The organizing at the Mesa location stemmed from, in part, a well-liked manager being terminated after whistle-blowing on Starbucks' anti-union plan.[[97]](#cite_note-97)

Starbucks temporarily closed two stores participating in the union drive in October for renovations. The company claimed these closures were unrelated to the unionization efforts.[[98]](#cite_note-vice_1021-98) Starbucks began working with [Littler Mendelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Littler_Mendelson "Littler Mendelson"), a self-described "union-busting firm", in October.[[99]](#cite_note-99)[[100]](#cite_note-100)[[101]](#cite_note-101) Starbucks requested that the National Labor Relations Board include all Buffalo Starbucks locations in the union vote, however, the NLRB rejected this argument and declared store by store elections.[[102]](#cite_note-102)[[95]](#cite_note-:0-95) Finally, on December 9, 2021, the workers at the Elmwood Avenue store became the first unionized Starbucks workers at a Starbucks owned location in the United States with a 19–8 vote. The Camp Road location voted 12–8 not to be in the union.[[87]](#cite_note-wsj_0921-87) Starbucks does have unionized locations in other countries.[[87]](#cite_note-wsj_0921-87) On December 13, workers at two Boston area locations petitioned the NLRB for union elections to be unionize with Workers United. The workers cited the win in Buffalo as inspiration for organizing. Workers in at least one location had most cards signed within a day.[[103]](#cite_note-103)

In February 2022, Starbucks fired seven workers in [Memphis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee") who had led the unionization effort and temporarily closed the store.[[104]](#cite_note-104) In August 2022, the National Labor Relations Board accused the company of illegally discriminating against unionized workers by refusing them wage and benefit increases and requesting restitution. It also asked that the CEO at the time, Howard Schultz, or a board official read a notice about this purportedly unlawful move.[[105]](#cite_note-105) That same month, unions were certified at 211 locations in the US.[[106]](#cite_note-106) On November 17, 2022, Starbucks’ annual Red Cup Day and one of the busiest days for employees, over 100 locations had employees go on strike. The workers were seeking higher staffing levels, better wages, and consistent schedules.[[107]](#cite_note-107)

Most unionization efforts are made through SBWU (Starbucks Workers United). There are over 9,000 American locations, but since the first unionized location in New York in 2021, less than 3% have voted to unionize. SBWU and Starbucks have yet to successfully negotiate a contract. Starbucks claims in a letter and on its website that the Workers United has delayed bargaining, has illegally broadcast bargaining sessions, refused to meet in person, and that Starbucks has reported more than 22 unfair labor practice charges to the NLRB (National Labor Relations Board).[[108]](#cite_note-108)[[109]](#cite_note-109) By March 2023, the NLRB found no merit in Starbucks's complaints and instead ruled that it was Starbucks who refused to bargain.[[110]](#cite_note-unions_March_2023_Vox-110)

On June 23, 2023, Starbucks workers at unionized stores went on strike over the company's stance on in-store [LGBT pride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_pride "LGBT pride") decorations.[[111]](#cite_note-111)

### Low calorie and sugar-free products

In January 2008, Starbucks began a "skinny" line of drinks, offering [lower-calorie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_calorie "Low calorie") and sugar-free versions of the company's offered drinks that use [skim milk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skim_milk "Skim milk"), and can be sweetened by a choice of natural sweeteners (such as [raw sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raw_sugar "Raw sugar"), [agave syrup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agave_syrup "Agave syrup"), or honey), [artificial sweeteners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_substitute "Sugar substitute") (such as [Sweet'N Low](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet'N_Low "Sweet'N Low"), [Splenda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splenda "Splenda"), [Equal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_(sweetener) "Equal (sweetener)")), or one of the company's [sugar-free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar-free "Sugar-free") syrup flavors.[[114]](#cite_note-114)[[115]](#cite_note-115)

### Non-dairy milk offerings

In 1997, Starbucks first offered non-dairy milk at its U.S. stores with the introduction of [soy milk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soy_milk "Soy milk").[[116]](#cite_note-116) In 2007, Starbucks stopped using milk originating from [rBGH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RBGH "RBGH")-treated cows.[[117]](#cite_note-117) The company also adopted a new dairy standard for all [espresso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espresso "Espresso")-based drinks, switching from whole to 2% reduced fat milk.[[118]](#cite_note-118) In 2015, Starbucks began serving [coconut milk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coconut_milk "Coconut milk").[[119]](#cite_note-119) In 2016, it began serving [almond milk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almond_milk "Almond milk").[[120]](#cite_note-120) In January 2020, [oat milk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oat_milk "Oat milk") became available nationally.[[121]](#cite_note-121)[[122]](#cite_note-Schouten-122) The company also offers non-dairy creamers at retail in partnership with Nestlé SA.[[122]](#cite_note-Schouten-122)

CEO Kevin Johnson said in a 2020 interview that, [milk substitutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milk_substitute "Milk substitute") would be a big part of reducing carbon emissions.[[123]](#cite_note-123) That effort has prompted vegans, environmentalists, people with lactose intolerance and others to urge the company to eliminate the upcharge for drinks made with dairy-free milk. [PETA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_for_the_Ethical_Treatment_of_Animals "People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals") encouraged sit-ins at Starbucks locations and purchased Starbucks stock to draw attention to what they believe is an unfair charge.[[124]](#cite_note-124) A Starbucks Canada spokesperson told ET Canada that customizations such as added flavours, non-dairy beverages or an additional shot of espresso, would incur an additional charge.[[125]](#cite_note-125)

In December 2020, Starbucks announced it would offer [Oatly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oatly "Oatly") oat milk in all US stores starting in spring 2021.[[126]](#cite_note-126) With the launch of their holiday menu in November 2024, Starbucks ended the upcharge for non-dairy milk additions to drinks.[[127]](#cite_note-127)

### Ethos water

[Ethos water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethos_water "Ethos water"), a brand of bottled water acquired by Starbucks in 2003, is sold at locations throughout North America. Ethos bottles feature prominent labeling stating "helping children get clean water", referring to the fact that US$0.05 from each US$1.80 bottle sold (US$0.10 per bottle in Canada) is used to fund clean water projects in underdeveloped areas. Although sales of Ethos water have raised over US$6.2 million for clean water efforts, the brand is not incorporated as a charity. Critics have argued that the claim on the label misleads consumers into thinking that Ethos is primarily a charitable organization when it is actually a for-profit brand and only 5 cents per bottle supports clean-water projects.[[128]](#cite_note-128)[[129]](#cite_note-129)

The founders of Ethos have stated that the brand is intended to raise awareness of third-world clean water issues and provide socially responsible consumers with an opportunity to support the cause by choosing Ethos over other brands.[[130]](#cite_note-130) Starbucks has since redesigned the American version of the Ethos water bottles, stating the amount of money donated per bottle in the description.[[131]](#cite_note-131)

### Instant coffee

In March 2009, Starbucks introduced a line of instant coffee packets, called VIA "Ready Brew".[[132]](#cite_note-132) It was first unveiled in New York City with subsequent testing of the product also in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"), [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), and [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"). The first two VIA flavors include Italian Roast and Colombia, which were then rolled out in October 2009, across the U.S. and Canada with Starbucks stores promoting the product with a [blind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_study "Blind study") "taste challenge" of the instant versus fresh roast, in which many people could not tell the difference between the instant and freshly brewed coffee. Financial analysts speculated that by introducing instant coffee, Starbucks would devalue its own brand.[[133]](#cite_note-133)

### Coffee makers and single-use capsules

In September 2012, Starbucks announced plans to introduce the Verismo, a consumer-grade single-serve coffee machine that uses sealed plastic cups of coffee grounds, and a "milk pod" for lattes.[[134]](#cite_note-134)

In November 2012, Starbucks Verismo became publicly available, consisting of a line of coffee makers that brew espresso and regular chocolate from coffee capsules, a type of pre-apportioned [single-use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disposable_product "Disposable product") container of ground coffee and flavourings utilizing the K-Fee pod system.[[135]](#cite_note-135)

In a brief review of the 580 model, [Consumer Reports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_Reports "Consumer Reports") described the results of a comparative test of the Verismo 580 against two competitive brands:

> Because you have to conduct a rinse cycle between each cup, the Verismo wasn't among the most convenient of single-serve machines in our coffeemaker tests. Other machines we've tested have more flexibility in adjusting brew-strength—the Verismo has buttons for coffee, espresso, and latte with no strength variation for any type. And since Starbucks has limited its coffee selection to its own brand, there are only eight varieties so far plus a milk pod for the latte.[*[excessive quote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Quotations#Specific_recommendations "Wikipedia:Quotations")*][[136]](#cite_note-136)

Panera Bread.content:
Panera offers a wide array of pastries and baked goods, such as bagels, brownies, cookies, croissants, muffins, and scones. These, along with Panera's artisan breads, are typically baked by an on-staff baker the day before serving. Aside from the bakery section, Panera has a regular menu for dine-in or takeout, including salads, sandwiches, side choices, and soups, as well as coffee, espresso drinks, frozen drinks, fruit smoothies, hot chocolate, iced drinks, lattes, lemonade, and tea. [...] is an American multinational chain of bakery-cafe fast casual restaurants with over 2,000 locations, all of which are in the United States and Canada. Its headquarters are in Fenton, Missouri. The chain operates as Saint Louis Bread Company in the Greater St. Louis area, with over 100 locations. **Panera Bread Company**[[7]](#cite_note-7) ([/pəˈnɛərə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*pə-NAIR-ə*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")) is an American multinational [chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_store "Chain store") of bakery-cafe [fast casual restaurants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_casual_restaurant "Fast casual restaurant") with over 2,000 locations, all of which are in the United States and Canada. Its [headquarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headquarters "Headquarters") are in [Fenton, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenton,_Missouri "Fenton, Missouri"). The chain operates as **Saint Louis Bread Company** in the [Greater St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_St._Louis "Greater St. Louis") area, with over 100 locations.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Panera offers a wide array of pastries and baked goods, such as bagels, brownies, cookies, croissants, muffins, and scones. These, along with Panera's [artisan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artisan "Artisan") breads, are typically baked by an on-staff baker the day before serving. Aside from the bakery section, Panera has a regular menu for dine-in or takeout, including salads, sandwiches, side choices, and soups, as well as coffee, [espresso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espresso "Espresso") drinks, frozen drinks, fruit smoothies, [hot chocolate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_chocolate "Hot chocolate"), iced drinks, [lattes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latte "Latte"), lemonade, and tea.[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)

Panera Bread, formerly owned by [Au Bon Pain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au_Bon_Pain "Au Bon Pain"), is currently owned by [JAB Holding Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JAB_Holding_Company "JAB Holding Company"), which is, in turn, owned by the Reimann family of Germany.[[11]](#cite_note-wsj-shaich-11) Panera was once the largest provider of free [Wi-Fi hotspots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi-Fi_hotspot "Wi-Fi hotspot") in the United States.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Ken and Linda Rosenthal founded the St. Louis Bread Company in 1987 after Ken visited [sourdough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sourdough "Sourdough") bakery-café La Boulanger in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") at the insistence of his brother. After being fascinated with the process of sourdough making, he was trained to make sourdough under instruction of the owner, Roger Brunello for a year.[[13]](#cite_note-NYTsandomir-13) The first location was opened in [Kirkwood, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirkwood,_Missouri "Kirkwood, Missouri"). The Rosenthals invested $150,000 and received a $150,000 [Small Business Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_Business_Administration "Small Business Administration") loan.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

Au Bon Pain Co., a [public company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_company "Public company"), purchased the St. Louis Bread Company in 1993 for $23 million.[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-gamble-17)

In 1997, Au Bon Pain changed the company name to Panera, from a word that has roots in the Latin word for "[breadbasket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadbasket "Breadbasket")" ([Classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_Latin "Classical Latin") *pānārium*, [Vulgar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgar_Latin "Vulgar Latin") *pānāria*) and is identical to the word for "breadbasket" in [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language") and [Catalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_language "Catalan language"). The original name was retained for locations in Missouri.[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[17]](#cite_note-gamble-17) At the same time, the St. Louis Bread Company renovated its 20 bakery-cafes in the St. Louis area.[[19]](#cite_note-About-19)[[17]](#cite_note-gamble-17)

In May 1999, Au Bon Pain Co. sold the Au Bon Pain chain to the firm [Bruckmann, Rosser, Sherrill & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruckmann,_Rosser,_Sherrill_&_Co. "Bruckmann, Rosser, Sherrill & Co.") for $78 million to focus on the Panera Bread chain.[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)

In 2000, Panera Bread moved its headquarters to [Richmond Heights, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond_Heights,_Missouri "Richmond Heights, Missouri").[[22]](#cite_note-22)

In 2007, Panera Bread purchased a 51% stake in [Paradise Bakery & Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradise_Bakery_&_Café "Paradise Bakery & Café"), a [Phoenix metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_metropolitan_area "Phoenix metropolitan area")-based concept with over 70 locations in 10 states, predominantly in the West and Southwest, for $21.1 million.[[23]](#cite_note-23) The company purchased the balance of Paradise in June 2009.[[19]](#cite_note-About-19)

### Expansion into Canada

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Expansion into Canada")]

In October 2008, Panera Bread expanded into [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), opening locations in [Richmond Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond_Hill,_Ontario "Richmond Hill, Ontario"), [Thornhill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thornhill,_Ontario "Thornhill, Ontario"), [Oakville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakville,_Ontario "Oakville, Ontario"), and [Mississauga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississauga,_Ontario "Mississauga, Ontario") in the [Greater Toronto Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Toronto_Area "Greater Toronto Area").[[24]](#cite_note-24)

A [class action lawsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_action_lawsuit "Class action lawsuit") was filed against the company in February 2008, alleging it failed to disclose material adverse facts about the company's financial well-being, business relationships, and prospects.[[25]](#cite_note-25) In February 2011, Panera agreed to pay $5.75 million to shareholders while admitting no wrongdoing, settling the lawsuit.[[26]](#cite_note-26)[[27]](#cite_note-27)

In November 2010, Panera Bread relocated its headquarters to Sunset Hills while vacating its Richmond Heights headquarters and [Brentwood, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentwood,_Missouri "Brentwood, Missouri") offices.[[28]](#cite_note-28) The company leased additional space for its headquarters in 2013.[[29]](#cite_note-29)

### Ordering and delivery

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Ordering and delivery")]

In May 2014, Panera unveiled "Panera 2.0", a series of integrated technologies including new capabilities for digital ordering, payment, operations, and consumption. It includes tablet kiosks with [iPads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPad "IPad"), which the company calls *Fast Lane*, where customers may place an order and pay without approaching the counter.[[30]](#cite_note-30)[[31]](#cite_note-31) Customers can also place orders and pay via an app on their smartphone or tablet.[[32]](#cite_note-32) In 2017, digital orders accounted for over $1 billion in orders or 26% of sales.[[33]](#cite_note-33)[[34]](#cite_note-34)

The company introduced delivery services in May 2018, servicing 897 cities in 43 states and employing its own drivers.[[35]](#cite_note-35)[[36]](#cite_note-36)[[37]](#cite_note-37) According to the company, this created 13,000 jobs.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

### Rebranding, acquisitions, and use of technology

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Rebranding, acquisitions, and use of technology")]

#### 2010s

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2010s")]

Every Paradise Bakery & Café location was rebranded in September 2015 as Panera Bread.[[39]](#cite_note-39)

In the fourth quarter of 2015, Panera acquired a majority stake in [Tatte Bakery & Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatte_Bakery_&_Café "Tatte Bakery & Café"), a bakery-cafe concept chain with locations in the [Boston area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Boston "Greater Boston"),[[40]](#cite_note-40)[[41]](#cite_note-41) later opening in metro [Washington D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_D.C. "Washington D.C.")[[42]](#cite_note-42)

On March 23, 2016, Panera opened its 2,000th location, a cafe in [Elyria, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elyria,_Ohio "Elyria, Ohio").[[43]](#cite_note-43)

In January 2017, Panera announced its food menu was free of artificial colors, flavors, sweeteners, and [preservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preservative "Preservative").[[44]](#cite_note-44)[[11]](#cite_note-wsj-shaich-11)

JAB Holding Company acquired the company on July 11, 2017, for $7.5 billion.[[11]](#cite_note-wsj-shaich-11)

On November 8, 2017, Panera announced that founder [Ron Shaich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Shaich "Ron Shaich") was stepping down as CEO, and company president Blaine Hurst would take over. Shaich remained chairman.[[45]](#cite_note-45) The company also announced the acquisition of [Au Bon Pain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au_Bon_Pain "Au Bon Pain").[[46]](#cite_note-acquire-46)[[11]](#cite_note-wsj-shaich-11)[[47]](#cite_note-47)[[48]](#cite_note-48)

Panera divested Tatte Bakery & Café to Act III Holdings, LLC, owned by Shaich in January 2018.[[49]](#cite_note-49)

In January 2018, the company formed a consulting business to help restaurants remove artificial ingredients from their menus.[[50]](#cite_note-50)[[51]](#cite_note-51)

On April 2, 2018, [Brian Krebs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Krebs "Brian Krebs") reported that the Panera Bread website had leaked between 7 million and 37 million customer records— including names, email, and physical addresses, customer loyalty account numbers, birthdays, and last four digits of the customers' credit card numbers— for at least eight months before the site was taken offline. Panera was notified privately about the vulnerability in August 2017 but failed to fix it until after it was disclosed publicly eight months later.[[52]](#cite_note-52)[[53]](#cite_note-53)[[54]](#cite_note-54) Panera said the leak affected fewer than 10,000 customers and had been fixed.[[55]](#cite_note-55)

#### 2020s

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2020s")]

On October 28, 2020, Panera announced they would add pizza to their menu to increase dinner options for customers.[[56]](#cite_note-56)

Panera announced on August 25, 2021, that it had merged with [Caribou Coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribou_Coffee "Caribou Coffee") and [Einstein Bros. Bagels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_Bros._Bagels "Einstein Bros. Bagels") to form Panera Brands.[[57]](#cite_note-57)

In August 2022, the company announced that it was testing the use of [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") in its drive-thru lanes via two locations in upstate New York. It used OpenCity's voice ordering technology, Tori. At the time of the announcement, roughly 45% of the chain's locations had drive-thru lanes. In making this move, the firm was joining other firms in the restaurant industry, like [McDonald's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonald's "McDonald's"), [Burger King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burger_King "Burger King"), and [Taco Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_Bell "Taco Bell"), and it came on top of other uses of artificial intelligence at the chain.[[58]](#cite_note-58)

In September 2022, Panera announced that legacy St. Louis Bread Co. locations outside [St. Louis City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis") and [St. Louis County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_County,_Missouri "St. Louis County, Missouri") would be rebranded as Panera when remodeled, with locations in the inner core of the [metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_St._Louis "Greater St. Louis") retaining the Bread Co. name.[[59]](#cite_note-59) One location in St. Louis County is named Panera as it is a prototype of the "Next Gen" restaurant design.[[60]](#cite_note-60)

In mid-2023, Panera moved its headquarters from Sunset Hills to [Fenton, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenton,_Missouri "Fenton, Missouri"), downsizing the square footage by more than half.[[61]](#cite_note-61) The move preceded two rounds of corporate layoffs in late 2023 and 2024.[[62]](#cite_note-62)

In December 2023, it was learned that Panera Bread confidentially filed to go public again. The company was last publicly traded in 2017 before being acquired by JAB Holding for $7.5 billion.[[63]](#cite_note-63)

In April 2024, Panera launched a major menu overhaul marketed as the "New Era at Panera," which the company described as the most significant menu transformation in its history.[[64]](#cite_note-64) The update involved discontinuing categories such as flatbread pizzas and grain bowls to refocus on core offerings like soups, salads, and sandwiches. The change introduced over 20 new or enhanced items with larger portions and lower price points in a strategic effort to improve value and increase customer traffic.[[65]](#cite_note-65)

On February 14, 2025, Ken Rosenthal, the founder of St. Louis Bread Company, died at age 81 due to complications from Alzheimer's disease.[[13]](#cite_note-NYTsandomir-13)

In March 2025, the company named Paul Carbone its new CEO.[[66]](#cite_note-wsjcarbone-66)

In July 2025, it was announced that the company was continuing a move begun in 2024 to a "par-baked" model for its restaurants, closing down existing dough-making facilities, and laying off employees. This model has restaurants receive partially-baked ("Par-baked") frozen bread which is finished in the store instead of freshly baked every day.[[67]](#cite_note-67) The company has also been reportedly rolling back their "clean food guidelines" which previously advocated for stances against antibiotics and hormones, and for animal welfare.[[68]](#cite_note-68)

## Social responsibility

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Social responsibility")]

### Panera Cares: non-profit restaurants

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Panera Cares: non-profit restaurants")]

In 2010, the company's nonprofit foundation created Panera Cares, a "[Pay what you can](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pay_what_you_can "Pay what you can")", pay it forward (PIF), and traditional charitable behavior[[69]](#cite_note-69) restaurant in its home market of St. Louis.[[70]](#cite_note-70) CEO Ron Shaich based the idea on an [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC") profile of the [SAME Cafe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAME_Cafe "SAME Cafe") in [Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver "Denver"), Colorado.[[71]](#cite_note-71) It later expanded the concept to [Dearborn, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dearborn,_Michigan "Dearborn, Michigan"); [Portland, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland,_Oregon "Portland, Oregon"); [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"); and [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston").[[72]](#cite_note-72)[[73]](#cite_note-73) Several of their sites served 3,500 customers weekly.[[74]](#cite_note-74) The Panera Cares in Chicago shut down at the end of January 2015.[[75]](#cite_note-75) The Panera Cares in Portland, Oregon shut down at the end of June 2016. The original location near St. Louis closed in January 2018.[[76]](#cite_note-76) The last location in Boston closed on February 15, 2019.[[77]](#cite_note-77)[[78]](#cite_note-78)

### Caged and cage-free eggs

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Caged and cage-free eggs")]

On November 5, 2015, Panera pledged that it would use only [cage-free eggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cage-free_eggs "Cage-free eggs") in all of its stores by 2020.[[79]](#cite_note-79) Panera also announced the addition of more plant-based proteins, such as [edamame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edamame "Edamame") and organic [quinoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quinoa "Quinoa"), to its menu. At the time of the announcement, the company said it was 21% cage-free in the roughly 70 million eggs it used in 2015.[[80]](#cite_note-80) In December 2016, it published its third animal welfare progress report, announcing new efforts to improve broiler chicken welfare.[[81]](#cite_note-81) In 2021, Panera announced that it had transitioned to cage-free eggs for 65% of its egg supply but not yet the remaining 35%.[[82]](#cite_note-82)

### Climate change

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Climate change")]

Panera Bread includes a "Cool Food" pledge in its campaign to "curb global warming".[[83]](#cite_note-choices-83) Panera Bread provides American consumers with dietary guidelines to help them change their eating patterns to help reduce carbon emissions. Through the Cool Foods pledge, the company uses traffic lights for different healthy and unhealthy foods. Foods labeled "green" are branded healthy, while those labeled "yellow" are warned to be consumed in moderation. In 2015, Panera Bread also announced its policy against the use of [genetically modified organisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetically_modified_food_controversies "Genetically modified food controversies") (GMOs), making it the first food chain in the country to question the safety and environmental friendliness of these foods.[[84]](#cite_note-84)

### Community giving

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Community giving")]

The Day-End Dough-Nation program provides unsold bread and baked goods to local area hunger relief agencies and charities. Panera Bread bakery-cafes donate $100 million worth of unsold bread and baked goods annually to local organizations.[[85]](#cite_note-85) Panera also supports events held by non-profit organizations serving those in need by donating a certificate or fresh bakery products.[[86]](#cite_note-86)

## Controversies and lawsuits

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Controversies and lawsuits")]

### Animal welfare issues and lawsuit

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Animal welfare issues and lawsuit")]

Panera Bread has been the subject of increased scrutiny regarding its [animal welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_welfare "Animal welfare") policies, particularly its sourcing of pork, dairy, and seafood. According to [Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuters "Reuters"), internal documents revealed that the company has loosened its ingredient standards, allowing the use of some antibiotics in pork and turkey and permitting animal byproducts in cattle and chicken feed.[[87]](#cite_note-87) Drawing on that report, a 2026 lawsuit by a food safety and animal welfare nonprofit alleged that Panera had misled customers about its animal welfare practices. The lawsuit claimed that Panera had marketed itself for its humane practices, including sourcing chicken from suppliers that provide sufficient living space for livestock, but that none of the chickens in its supply chain came from suppliers who met the standard.[[88]](#cite_note-88)

### Violation of California Labor Code

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Violation of California Labor Code")]

In 2009 and 2011, class-action lawsuits were filed by former workers, alleging that the company violated the [California Labor Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Labor_Code "California Labor Code"), failed to pay [overtime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overtime "Overtime"), failed to provide meal and rest periods, failed to pay employees upon termination, and violated California's [Unfair Competition Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unfair_Competition_Law "Unfair Competition Law"). Panera paid $5 million to settle all claims and denied any wrongdoing.[[89]](#cite_note-89)[[90]](#cite_note-90)

### Racial discrimination allegation (2011)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Racial discrimination allegation (2011)")]

In 2011, a former employee filed a [racial discrimination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_discrimination "Racial discrimination") lawsuit alleging that he was fired after repeatedly having a Black man work the cash register instead of putting him in a less visible location, and assigning "pretty young girls" as the cashiers, as requested by supervisors.[[91]](#cite_note-Mirando-91)[[92]](#cite_note-92) The plaintiff also said he was fired after requesting another month off after returning from three months of [sick leave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sick_leave "Sick leave").[[91]](#cite_note-Mirando-91) Panera said that it "does not discriminate based on national origin, race or sex" and that the plaintiff "was terminated because he had used all of his medical leave and was unable to return to work".[[91]](#cite_note-Mirando-91) The plaintiff worked in a store owned by franchisee Sam Covelli,[[93]](#cite_note-93) who also owns the stores that were involved in the 2003 racial discrimination lawsuit.[[94]](#cite_note-94)[[95]](#cite_note-95) Covelli Enterprises is the single largest franchisee of Panera Bread with nearly 300 stores in Ohio, Pennsylvania, West Virginia, and Florida.[[96]](#cite_note-96) The lawsuit was settled in June 2012.[[97]](#cite_note-97)

### Peanut butter allergy

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Peanut butter allergy")]

In 2016, a lawsuit was filed after an employee at a [Natick, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natick,_Massachusetts "Natick, Massachusetts"), store put peanut butter on a sandwich, despite being informed that the person receiving the sandwich had a [peanut allergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut_allergy "Peanut allergy"). The plaintiffs charged the company and those employees involved with [intentional infliction of emotional distress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intentional_infliction_of_emotional_distress "Intentional infliction of emotional distress") and [negligent infliction of emotional distress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negligent_infliction_of_emotional_distress "Negligent infliction of emotional distress"), as well as [assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_(crime) "Assault (crime)") and [battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_(crime) "Battery (crime)").[[98]](#cite_note-peanut-98) The recipient of the sandwich was hospitalized briefly.[[99]](#cite_note-99)

### Class action for failure to pay overtime wages (2017)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Class action for failure to pay overtime wages (2017)")]

In December 2017, former employees filed a [class action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_action "Class action") lawsuit against the company, claiming they were not paid overtime wages.[[100]](#cite_note-100)

### *Tabler v. Panera LLC et al*

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Tabler v. Panera LLC et al")]

In March 2019, Plaintiff Brianna Tabler in California filed a class-action lawsuit, accusing Panera of false advertising and fraud. While Panera's former CEO Ron Schaich claimed that Panera's menus continue to be completely void of artificial flavors, sweeteners, and ingredients,[[101]](#cite_note-biclean-101) Tabler argues against the company's intentional redaction of the fact that their products contain traces of the synthetic biocide [glyphosate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glyphosate "Glyphosate").[[102]](#cite_note-102) In October 2019, Judge [Lucy Koh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_Koh "Lucy Koh") granted a motion to dismiss the lawsuit. Tabler filed an amended complaint in November 2019, to which Panera filed in January 2020 another motion to dismiss.[[103]](#cite_note-103) Tabler filed a motion to voluntarily dismiss the complaint on July 30, 2020, closing the case.[[104]](#cite_note-VolDismissal-104)

### Charged Lemonade lawsuits

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Charged Lemonade lawsuits ")]

On September 10, 2022, 21-year-old Sarah Katz, a student at the University of Pennsylvania, purchased and consumed a "supercharged" lemonade drink from a Panera location in Philadelphia. Allegedly, Katz was unaware of the high [caffeine content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caffeine "Caffeine") of the drinks, which has been criticized as extremely dangerous; a 20-US-fluid-ounce (590 ml) Panera Charged Lemonade contained 260 mg of caffeine, equivalent to four [espresso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espresso "Espresso") shots, and the 30-ounce (890 mL) lemonade contained 390 mg (six espressos).[[105]](#cite_note-105)[[106]](#cite_note-106)[[107]](#cite_note-107) Katz suffered from [Long QT Type 1 Syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_QT_syndrome "Long QT syndrome"), a heart condition that can result in an irregular heartbeat in certain situations. On the same day, Katz went into [cardiac arrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiac_arrest "Cardiac arrest") while at another restaurant and was transported to the Pennsylvania Presbyterian Hospital, where she suffered another arrest and was then pronounced dead.[[108]](#cite_note-KvP-108)

In October 2023, Katz's parents sued Panera for the [wrongful death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrongful_death_claim "Wrongful death claim") of their daughter caused by misleading labeling and description of the drink.[[108]](#cite_note-KvP-108) Later in October, amid reports that dispensers had been moved behind the counter to limit access, Panera changed labeling for the drink, noting its caffeine content and need for moderation, and warning potentially sensitive consumers.[[109]](#cite_note-109)

In December 2023, a second individual was reported as having died after consuming Panera's Charged Lemonade. The individual, Dennis Brown, died at age 46 after reportedly consuming three servings of Charged Lemonade at a Panera location in [Fleming Island, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleming_Island,_Florida "Fleming Island, Florida"). Brown had high blood pressure, a developmental delay, [attention deficit hyperactivity disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_deficit_hyperactivity_disorder "Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder") (ADHD), and a chromosomal disorder that caused a mild intellectual disability and blurry vision, according to a wrongful death lawsuit filed by family members.[[110]](#cite_note-110)[[111]](#cite_note-111) Social media commentators began to nickname the drink "the lemonade that kills you".[[112]](#cite_note-112)[[113]](#cite_note-auto-113)

The caffeine content was later reduced by Panera in December 2023, with the 30-ounce drink reduced to 237 mg and the 20-ounce to 158 mg.[[113]](#cite_note-auto-113) In May 2024, the company announced they would begin phasing out the drink.[[114]](#cite_note-114)

### Delivery costs

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Delivery costs")]

In February 2024, Panera settled a [class-action lawsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class-action_lawsuit "Class-action lawsuit") for $2 million, which accused the company a year beforehand of misleading customers from 2020 to 2021 about its costs for delivery orders. Panera did not admit fault in the settlement.[[115]](#cite_note-115)

### 2026 Data breach and class action

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Panera_Bread&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: 2026 Data breach and class action")]

On January 28, 2026, Panera Bread was hit by a cyber attack, along with other companies including [Bumble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bumble "Bumble") and [Match](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Match.com "Match.com"). The company revealed that contact information was the data involved.[[116]](#cite_note-116) Later reporting noted that the aggressor was [ShinyHunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ShinyHunters "ShinyHunters"), that they stole information on around 5 million people (14 million records), and subsequently leaked this information to the [dark web](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_web "Dark web").[[117]](#cite_note-117) Two class action lawsuits were filed against the company shortly after, citing Panera Bread's failure to properly secure the personal information that was stolen.[[118]](#cite_note-118)

Krispy Kreme.content:
Krispy Kreme, Inc. (previously Krispy Kreme Doughnuts, Inc.) is an American multinational doughnut company and coffeehouse chain. Krispy Kreme was founded by Vernon Rudolph (1915–1973), who bought a yeast-raised recipe from a New Orleans chef, rented a building in 1937 in what is now historic Old Salem in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, and began selling to local grocery stores. Steady growth preceded an ambitious expansion as a public company in the period 2000 to 2016, which ultimately proved [...] On January 12, 2017, Krispy Kreme opened its first store in Panama City, Panama.

On January 27, 2018, Krispy Kreme opened its first store in Guatemala City, Guatemala. On February 28, 2018, Krispy Kreme opened its first store in Manukau, Auckland, New Zealand. On March 10, 2018, Krispy Kreme opened its first store in Ikeja City Mall, Lagos, Nigeria. On September 26, 2018, Krispy Kreme opened its first store in Dublin, Ireland, which has since become the most profitable store worldwide. [...] In February 2015, a Krispy Kreme branch in Kingston upon Hull, England, announced during the half-term break of schools that it was launching, among other events that week, "Krispy Kreme Klub Wednesday", during which children could decorate doughnuts. However, it attracted controversy after it was promoted as "KKK Wednesday" on Facebook, due to it sharing an abbreviation with the Ku Klux Klan, an American white supremacist group.
